question: A 65-year-old African-American man presents to your office with dysphagia. He reports that he has found it progressively more difficult to swallow food over the past year. At the time of presentation, he is able to eat only soup. Social history is significant for asbestos exposure, multiple daily drinks of hard alcohol, and a 70 pack-year smoking history. What would you most expect to see on an esophageal biopsy of this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "65-year-old African-American man" -> "progressive dysphagia" -> "risk factors: asbestos exposure, alcohol use, smoking" -> "increased risk for esophageal cancer" -> "possible squamous cell carcinoma" -> "esophageal biopsy shows keratin nests and pearls" -> 85%

CHAIN: "65-year-old African-American man" -> "progressive dysphagia" -> "history of heavy smoking and alcohol use" -> "possible esophageal squamous cell carcinoma" -> "esophageal biopsy shows keratin nests and pearls" -> 80%

CHAIN: "65-year-old African-American man" -> "dysphagia for solid food" -> "risk factors include asbestos exposure" -> "possible development of esophageal cancer" -> "esophageal biopsy shows keratin nests and pearls" -> 75%

CHAIN: "65-year-old African-American man" -> "dysphagia" -> "long history of smoking and alcohol" -> "increased risk for esophageal malignancy" -> "esophageal biopsy shows keratin nests and pearls" -> 70%
analysis: The patient's history of progressive dysphagia, significant smoking and alcohol use, and asbestos exposure raises suspicion for esophageal cancer, particularly squamous cell carcinoma, which is more common in African-American men. On biopsy, one would expect to see keratin nests and pearls, which are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma. Glandular metaplasia (Barrett's esophagus) is more associated with adenocarcinoma, which is less likely given the patient's risk factors and presentation.
